# Verification â€” Per-Finding Refutation Pass

Shared reference for audit skills (`owasp-audit`, `api-audit`, `business-logic-testing`, `web-pentest`) and for
`finding-triage`. Every candidate finding goes through this pass **before** it reaches `findings.json` or a report.
The goal is to try to disprove the candidate, then close it with one of three verdicts.

The pass works because the person checking a finding is not the person who found it. Someone who wrote the candidate
tends to re-read their own reasoning instead of the code. A verifier that only sees the claim and the cited lines
reads the code.

## Two stages: fixed exclusions, then the verifier

False positives get filtered twice, in this order.

**Stage 1: fixed exclusion rules.** Before any verifier runs, drop the candidates that match a rule below. The rules
are mechanical and the same on every run, so two runs over the same code drop the same candidates. Apply them by where
the code lives and whether it ships, never by how likely the bug looks.

| Rule | Drops a candidate in | Unless |
|---|---|---|
| Test code | `test/`, `tests/`, `spec/`, `__tests__/`, `*.test.*`, `*.spec.*`, `*_test.go`, `test_*.py` | Production code imports it, the route or handler is mounted in the deployed build, or the build ships the file |
| Fixtures and sample data | `fixtures/`, `testdata/`, `__mocks__/`, seed files for local dev | The deployed environment loads it (a production seed, a default config read at boot) |
| Generated code | Files marked `Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT` or `@generated`, compiled output (`dist/`, `build/`, `.next/`) | Never. Raise it against the generator input or template instead, which is where the fix goes |
| Vendored and third-party code | `vendor/`, `node_modules/`, `third_party/`, copied-in libraries | The repo has modified the copy. An unmodified copy is a version question for `dependency-audit` |
| Docs and examples | `*.md`, `docs/`, `examples/`, snippets in comments | The example is deployed, or the repo's own code copies it |
| Documented hardening note | The gap is already on the run's hardening-notes list | The candidate brings a traced impact the note didn't have. Then it's a new candidate |
| Prior rejection | The fingerprint matches a `rejected` record from the last run | The code at `ruled_out_by.location` changed. Then it's a new candidate |

Some things are never excluded by location. A credential that looks live is a finding wherever it sits, including a
test fixture (`secrets-audit` owns it). CI workflow files run with real tokens, so they are not "config". A debug or
test route is in scope as soon as the deployed build serves it.

Record what stage 1 dropped and which rule dropped it: a count per rule in the report, and, where the skill keeps a
coverage ledger, an `out_of_scope` unit whose check names the rule. Excluded candidates get no `findings.json` record.

**Stage 2: the per-finding verifier.** Every candidate that survives stage 1 goes through the pass below. The verifier
does not invent new exclusions. "It's probably test code" is a stage 1 question with a fixed answer, not a reason a
verifier can give.

This repo deliberately does not drop whole bug classes in stage 1. Some filters exclude every denial-of-service,
rate-limiting or open-redirect report outright. Several skills here report those and calibrate severity instead (see
`severity-calibration.md`), so class-level filtering would hide real findings.

## When to run it

- After the checklist / hunting phase, once per candidate. Don't batch several candidates into one verifier: a
  verifier that rejects one candidate tends to wave the next one through.
- **Small targets** (a few thousand lines, a dozen or more candidates): one verifier per candidate can mean 20
  subagents for a 150-line app. There you may group candidates that share no code path, up to about five per
  verifier, with each candidate written up and closed separately. Two candidates stay in separate verifiers when they
  touch the same handler or control, or when either one would be confirmed at High or Critical.
- Again whenever a verdict would move **up** (rejected â†’ needs_validation, needs_validation â†’ confirmed, or a
  severity increase) or the evidence changes materially. **An upgrade needs a new, independent verifier.** The verifier
  that produced the lower verdict does not get to overturn itself.
- On re-runs, for every carried-forward confirmed finding whose code changed (see `orchestration.md` where present).

A downgrade (confirmed â†’ needs_validation, or a lower severity) can be applied directly. Record why.

## How to run it

**With subagents** (Claude Code `Task`/Agent tool, or any platform that can spawn an isolated agent): spawn one fresh
verifier per candidate. Give it **only**:

1. The candidate record: title, claimed location, `trace[]`, `evidence[]`, and the claimed impact
2. Read access to the repository
3. The verdict definitions and the "does NOT rule out" list below
4. The record shape it must return (see `findings-format.md` where present)

Do **not** pass the hunter's reasoning, chat history, or the rest of the report.

In Claude Code with this plugin installed, use the plugin's `finding-verifier` subagent. It carries this procedure, the
rationalizations table below and the return shape, and it has only `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob`. Give it one candidate per
call. Other platforms use the template below.

**Without subagents** (single-context agents, Cursor, Codex): run the pass as a separate, explicit step after hunting
is finished. For each candidate, start from the cited `file:line` and re-derive the path from scratch. Don't re-read
your own earlier notes about the candidate until you have written down a verdict.

### Verifier prompt (template)

Adapt this to the platform. Keep the substance.

```text
You are verifying a security finding that someone else wrote. Assume it is wrong until the code proves otherwise.
Your job is to refute it.

Candidate:
<candidate record: title, location, trace[], evidence[], claimed impact>

Do this:
1. Open every file:line cited in trace[] and evidence[]. Confirm each line says what the candidate claims.
   If a cited line does not exist or says something else, note it.
2. Walk the path from the entrypoint to the sink. At each hop, list every control that could stop the attack:
   middleware, auth/ownership checks, validation, type coercion, framework escaping, database constraints,
   platform config in the repo.
3. Name the STRONGEST control you found. For that control, decide: does it run on EVERY path an attacker can reach
   before the sink, at the right time, and fail closed?
4. Decide whether the claimed impact actually follows. Who is the lower-trust principal, what boundary is crossed,
   and what concrete result occurs?
5. Return exactly one verdict: confirmed | needs_validation | rejected, with the fields listed for that verdict.
   Fill `counterevidence` with what you tried and what you found, even when the verdict is confirmed.
```

## The three verdicts

| Verdict | Bar | Required fields | Severity? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `confirmed` | A complete trace from attacker-controlled entrypoint â†’ (missing or bypassable control) â†’ sink â†’ concrete impact, **or** a working proof-of-concept against an environment you're authorized to test | `trace[]` (entrypoint first, sink last), `evidence[]`, `counterevidence`, `confidence`, `severity`, `conditions[]` | Yes |
| `needs_validation` | The code supports the claim, but **one decisive fact lives outside the code**: proxy or CDN behaviour, IdP settings, deploy-time env, a managed-service default, the headers a deployed origin actually sends | `blockers[]` (each names the exact unknown fact), `validation_plan` (a check the owner can run), `counterevidence`, `confidence` | **No.** Severity is assigned only after the blocker resolves to confirmed |
| `rejected` | A **specific named control, at a specific location**, runs on **every** path an attacker can reach before the sink and fails closed | `ruled_out_by {control, location}`, `counterevidence` | No |

### confirmed

- The trace has to be complete. "User input reaches `exec()`" is not a trace until you show where the input enters,
  each hop, and why nothing on the way stops it.
- `confidence` is honest. **A static-only trace caps at `medium`.** `high` needs a reproduced PoC, a failing test, or
  equivalent runtime evidence, recorded as `"reproduced": true` (the validator rejects `high` without it). Missing deployment evidence lowers confidence; it does not lower the severity floor of
  what the code demonstrably does.
- Severity follows [severity-calibration.md](severity-calibration.md): likelihood Ã— impact, and `overall â‰¤ impact`. If you can't state the
  concrete damage, the severity is lower than it feels.
- Record `conditions[]` that limit exploitation (`authentication_level`, `authorization_role`, `user_interaction`,
  `system_configuration`, `network_routing`, `environmental_dependency`, `data_state`, `timing_dependency`,
  `third_party_dependency`).

### needs_validation

This replaces the old "Potential" label. It is **not** a parking place for a hunch. Use it only when the code really does
support the claim and a single external fact decides it.

- Each `blockers[]` entry names one fact: "Whether Vercel strips `x-forwarded-host` before it reaches the app",
  not "deployment config unknown".
- `validation_plan` is a check the **owner** can run, local and/or against their deployment, with the expected result
  for each outcome. Example:

  ```text
  Run against your production origin:  curl -sI https://app.example.com/embed | grep -iE 'x-frame-options|content-security-policy'
  If both `frame-ancestors *` and `X-Frame-Options: DENY` appear â†’ confirmed (contradictory framing policy).
  If only one appears â†’ rejected; ruled out by the deployed header set.
  ```

- If you can't write a blocker and a plan, the candidate is either confirmed (you already know enough) or it's a
  hardening note or a rejected claim. It isn't needs_validation.

### rejected

- Name the control and where it lives: `ruled_out_by: { control: "requireOrgMember() guard", location:
  "src/server/trpc.ts:41" }`. "Looks safe" or "framework handles it" is not a rejection.
- The control must sit on **every** reachable path, run **before** the sink, and **fail closed**.
- Keep rejected records in `findings.json`. Re-runs read them so the same claim isn't raised again. A rejection
  suppresses **only that exact claim** (same fingerprint). A sibling path or a changed control is a new candidate.

Some rejections have no guard to point at. `ruled_out_by` then names the fact that rules the claim out and
`location` points at the evidence for it:

| Why it's ruled out | `control` | `location` |
|---|---|---|
| Never reached: the vulnerable function or package is never called | "`_.template` is never called; lodash is used only for `merge` and `pick`" | The only import or call site of the package. If nothing imports it, the line in the manifest or lockfile that declares it |
| Known-inert value: a vendor's published example key, a documented test card, a placeholder | "AWS's documented example access key ID; it can't authenticate" | The line where the value appears |
| Control inside a dependency: the library's own guard runs on every path | "jsonwebtoken 9.0.2 `verify()` rejects `alg: none` when a secret is given" | The lockfile or manifest line that pins that version |

A control inside a dependency rejects only when the installed version is pinned and that version's behaviour is the
one you checked: read in the vendored or installed source, the changelog, or the advisory's fixed-in version. If the
range in the manifest could resolve to a version without the guard and there's no lockfile, it's `needs_validation`
with the resolved version as the blocker. "The library probably handles it" is not a rejection (see below).

## What does NOT rule out a candidate

None of these is a reason to reject. Each one is a reason to keep looking:

- **General trust in a library or framework** ("Prisma parameterizes", "React escapes") without checking that this call
  site uses the safe API. Raw-query escape hatches and `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` exist for a reason.
- **A control on a different path.** The REST route checks ownership. The server action that writes the same table
  doesn't.
- **A control that runs at the wrong time.** Validation after the side effect, auth checked at enqueue but not in the
  worker, a signature verified after the body was already stored.
- **A control that can fail open.** Unset env var interpolation, `catch {}` around the check, a rate limiter that
  allows on Redis error, a feature flag defaulting to off.
- **A safe sibling.** Three handlers use the guard. That says nothing about the fourth.
- **Missing information.** "I couldn't find where this is called" is a blocker or an unresolved coverage item. It isn't
  a rejection.
- **Difficulty.** "Requires guessing a UUID" or "requires a race" lowers likelihood. It doesn't remove the finding.
- **The setting is operator-configurable.** If the shipped default is unsafe, the default is the finding (see "Unsafe
  shipped defaults" below).
- **"It's internal."** Internal services get reached through SSRF, compromised neighbours, and misrouted ingress.
  Record the network assumption as a `network_routing` condition instead.
- **Tests pass.** Tests check intended behaviour, not adversarial input.

## Rationalizations to reject

The list above says what can't close a candidate. This table is for the verifier's own reasoning, in both directions.
Each row is an argument that feels like a conclusion but isn't one, and the evidence that would actually settle it.
When you notice yourself making one of these arguments, go and get that evidence. If you can't get it, the
argument doesn't change the verdict.

Models in particular lean toward seeing bugs and toward rating them high. The verifier's default is that the candidate
is wrong. A verifier can also overcorrect, and wave things through to get to a clean report. Both columns matter.

**Arguments for keeping or inflating a candidate**

| Rationalization | What settles it |
|---|---|
| "This pattern is dangerous, so it's a vulnerability" | A trace from an attacker-reachable entrypoint to this call site, with the attacker's value still able to do harm when it gets there. A dangerous sink with no reachable input is not a finding |
| "An attacker could theoreticallyâ€¦" | Name the lower-trust principal, the exact input they send, and the line where it enters. Every "if" in the story is either shown in the code, recorded as a `conditions[]` entry, or written as a `needs_validation` blocker |
| "This is clearly critical" | The concrete damage, stated in one sentence, and the High/Critical acceptance checks in `severity-calibration.md`. `overall` stays at or below the impact you can show |
| "The same bug is in the sibling handler" | This call site, read on its own. A sibling's bug doesn't transfer, any more than a sibling's guard does |
| "It could matter if chained" | Each link in the chain shown in the code. Any unproven link makes it a blocker or a hardening note |
| "There's no input validation here" | What the sink does with the values that can actually reach it. A missing check on a value that's already typed, bounded or mapped through an allow-list may have no impact |
| "The scanner, the report or the code comment says it's vulnerable" | The code that runs. Claim text, `TODO: fix auth` comments and rule names are leads, not evidence |

**Arguments for dismissing a candidate**

| Rationalization | What settles it |
|---|---|
| "The framework probably escapes this" | This call site uses the safe API: auto-escaping is on in the config you can see and this output isn't marked raw, or the query goes through the parameterized builder rather than a raw-query method. Name the file and line |
| "There's probably a WAF, gateway or proxy in front" | The rule in the repo or IaC, applied to this route. If it lives outside the repo, it's `needs_validation` with the rule as the blocker. Never `rejected` on "probably" |
| "It's only internal" | Network policy, ingress or security-group config in the repo showing no path from the lower-trust principal. Without it, record a `network_routing` condition and keep the verdict |
| "The test suite would have caught it" | A test that sends this adversarial input to this path, asserts it's refused, and runs in CI. Cite its file and line. Even then, it settles only the path it exercises |
| "It's validated upstream" | The validator's file and line, shown to run on every path to this sink, before the sink, and to fail closed. That's the `rejected` bar. Short of it, keep looking |
| "The UI never sends that value" | A server-side check. Clients are attacker-controlled, so what the form allows proves nothing |
| "It's behind auth" | Authentication isn't authorization. Show the ownership or role check, or the finding stands with an `authentication_level` condition |
| "Only admins can reach it" | The role check's location, then ask whether the admin crosses any boundary (another tenant, a higher role, the host). Admin to admin on the admin's own data is no boundary. Admin to another tenant is |
| "The IDs are UUIDs, nobody can guess them" | Whether the IDs leak through list endpoints, URLs, logs, emails or referrers. Difficulty lowers likelihood. It doesn't reject |
| "This code looks unused" | The never-reached row of the table under "rejected": no call site, route not mounted. Point at the evidence. "Looks unused" alone is a blocker, not a rejection |
| "I already rejected something like this" | Nothing. Each candidate is checked on its own facts. This is why candidates get one verifier each |

## Unsafe shipped defaults

A hard-coded fallback secret (`process.env.JWT_SECRET || "changeme"`), a debug flag that defaults on, or a permissive
default config is **`confirmed`**, not `needs_validation`, whichever skill finds it. The code shows what happens
whenever the setting is missing, and missing is the state a new deployment starts in.

- Record a `system_configuration` condition: "deployments that don't set `JWT_SECRET`, or set it empty".
- Rate severity by what the default gives an attacker, as if it were live. Whether production overrides it is a
  deployment fact you can't see, so it caps `confidence` at `medium`. It doesn't lower the verdict or the severity.
- Put the owner's check (is the variable set, and to what length) in the finding's fix-verification text, not in a
  `validation_plan`.
- If you *can* see the deployment and it sets a strong value, the record is still `confirmed`, since a fresh deploy
  or a new environment gets the default. Rate likelihood lower and say why.

The same root cause should get the same verdict and severity from every skill that sees it. A hard-coded JWT fallback
that lets anyone forge an admin token is an authentication bypass to any account, wherever it's reported.

## Hardening notes are not verdicts

If the verifier finds the gap is real but there's **no traced impact** (Layer A already stops the attack and Layer B is
missing; a missing header with no exploit path; a checklist deviation), close the candidate as a **Hardening note**. It
goes in the report's "Hardening notes (not findings)" section with no severity. It gets no `findings.json` record.
Keep hardening notes in a short list next to the JSON (for example `hardening-notes.md` in the audit output directory)
so the report can render them. The coverage unit that produced the note can still be `covered`.

If a hardening note later picks up a traced impact (say, a missing CSP turns out to matter because a stored XSS sink
exists), it becomes a new candidate and goes through this pass.

## Live probing

Live checks stay allowed **when authorized**. For example, `curl -I` against the user's own deployed origin, or
confirming that a leaked key is live as part of secrets triage. The rules:

1. The authorization check of the consuming skill applies to the live target, not just the source. Only probe hosts
   the user owns or is authorized to test, and only with non-destructive requests (`HEAD`/`GET`, no state changes, no
   real customer credentials).
2. **A check you describe but don't run is a `needs_validation` item.** Write the exact command into
   `validation_plan`. Don't mark it confirmed or rejected on the strength of what the config file "should" produce.
3. A check you actually ran becomes evidence. Record the command, timestamp, and relevant response lines in
   `evidence[]` / `counterevidence`, then close the verdict normally.
4. For paired evidence (baseline request next to attack request), see `web-pentest`.

## Output of the pass

For each candidate, one record with the verdict-specific fields above, ready to be written to `findings.json`. The
consuming skill writes `findings.json`, validates it (`validate-findings.mjs` where present), and renders the report
from it. Prose never changes a verdict, severity, blocker, or demonstrated impact. If the report and the JSON disagree,
the JSON wins and the report is regenerated.

# Orchestration â€” Modes, Run Profiles, Hunters, and Re-runs

Shared reference for `owasp-audit` and `api-audit`. Use it when an audit is too big for one pass, or when the user asks
for a full audit. It assumes the recon and ledger from [recon-and-coverage.md](recon-and-coverage.md), the verdicts from [verification.md](verification.md),
and the record format in [findings-format.md](findings-format.md).

A single audit pass finds a fraction of what repeated, independent passes find. Cloudflare reports that one run
surfaced roughly half of what several runs found together. Splitting the work and repeating it is how you close that
gap. The evidence bar stays the same.

## Operating modes

| Mode | When | Output |
|---|---|---|
| **Guidance** (default) | The user asks a question, wants a quick look at a file or feature, or wants to know how to secure something | Conversational answer. Findings still follow the verdict rules. No ledger required |
| **Full audit** | The user explicitly asks for an audit / security review of a codebase, a PR, or a release | Recon â†’ ledger â†’ hunting â†’ verification â†’ critic â†’ `findings.json` â†’ report |

If the request is ambiguous ("can you check this for security issues?" on a whole repo), ask one question first: *"Do
you want a quick guidance pass, or a full audit with a coverage ledger and a findings.json report?"* Then proceed.

## Run profiles

Ask which profile, or pick one and say so. The report header names the profile.

| Profile | Hunting | Critic | Verification | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `quick` | One wave over the highest-priority units | One critic wave; leftovers become `deferred` | One independent verifier per candidate | Pre-launch smoke check, small app, time-boxed |
| `standard` | Waves until every in-scope unit is `covered`, `candidate`, `not_applicable`, or justified `deferred` | Repeat until a wave adds nothing high-value | One verifier per candidate, and a new one for any upgrade | Default full audit |
| `deep` | As standard, plus a Wildcard and an Obvious-things hunter, plus a second independent hunter on high-value boundaries | Repeat until a critic wave returns **no** missing units | As standard; also re-verify every confirmed high/critical with a second verifier | Pre-raise diligence, regulated data, after an incident |

**Profiles change breadth and redundancy, never the evidence bar.** A `quick` run doesn't get to confirm anything on a
weaker trace. It just covers less and says so: a `quick` run with deferred units is reported as **partial**.

## Coordinator and hunters

With subagents (Claude Code's Agent/Task tool, or similar), split the work:

- **Coordinator** (the main agent): runs recon, owns `architecture.md`, `coverage.json`, and `findings.json`, assigns
  units, runs critics and verifiers, renders the report. **Only the coordinator writes shared state.** Hunters return
  results; the coordinator merges them.
- **Hunters**: isolated subagents, each assigned a batch of ledger units (group by surface Ã— boundary so one hunter sees
  a whole boundary, for example "every surface that crosses tenant isolation").

**Assignment order:** unauthenticated surfaces first, then high-value boundaries (tenant isolation, admin, payments,
paid third-party work, file handling), then changed code (recent commits, the diff), then everything else.

Give every hunter the same structure. Paraphrase freely, but keep each part:

      "evidence": [{ "file": "...", "line": 0, "description": "..." }],

- **Wildcard.** Gets the architecture and the whole surface list but **no attack-class assignment**. Asked: "What would

- **Obvious things.** Literal and thorough: hard-coded secrets, debug flags, `eval`, disabled TLS verification, wildcard
  CORS, default credentials, admin routes without auth. It still has to trace impact. "`VERIFY_NONE` exists" is a
  hardening note until it reaches something that matters.

## Sequential fallback (no subagents)

On platforms without subagents (Cursor, Codex, or a single long session), run the same phases in order and keep the
isolation as best you can:

1. Recon â†’ write `architecture.md` and `coverage.json` (all `planned`).
2. Hunt unit-batch by unit-batch in the assignment order. After each batch, update the ledger **before** starting the
   next one, so the ledger, not your memory, holds what's done.
3. Finish **all** hunting before verifying. Then verify each candidate from its cited lines, without re-reading your
   hunting notes first (see [verification.md](verification.md)).
4. Run the critic as a separate step that reads only `architecture.md`, `coverage.json`, and the code.
5. Write and validate `findings.json`, then render the report.

If context runs low, stop at a unit boundary, mark the remaining units `deferred`, and report the run as partial. Don't
compress the evidence bar to finish.

## Re-runs and carry-forward

At the start of every full audit, look for a prior `security-audit/findings.json` and `coverage.json`.

| Prior record | Code at its trace/evidence locations | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `confirmed` | Unchanged | Carry forward by fingerprint. Re-verify (a quick verifier pass that the cited lines still say the same thing). Keep the disposition |
| `confirmed` | Changed | Revalidate with a fresh verifier. If the fix landed, close it as `Fixed` and keep the record. If the change moved code, update locations; the fingerprint stays the same |
| `needs_validation` | Any | Ask whether the owner ran the `validation_plan`. If yes, close on their result. If no, carry forward unchanged |
| `rejected` | Unchanged control | Suppress **that exact claim** (same fingerprint). Don't re-raise it |
| `rejected` | Control changed or removed | The rejection no longer holds. It's a new candidate |
| `covered` unit | Reviewed paths unchanged | Optionally skip in `quick`; re-review in `standard`/`deep` (different hunters find different things) |
| `covered` unit | Reviewed paths changed | Back to `planned` |

Find changes with `git diff --name-only <prior-audit-commit>..HEAD` (record the commit in `architecture.md` on every
run). Fingerprints identify the root cause, never line numbers, severity, or verdict, so they survive edits. A rejected
fingerprint suppresses only itself. A sibling with the same pattern on a different path is a different fingerprint.

## Cost and budget

Subagent fan-out multiplies token cost. Before a `standard` or `deep` run on a large repo, tell the user roughly how
many units and hunters you plan to use and confirm. If the budget runs out mid-run, the remaining units become
`deferred` and the report says partial.

# Severity calibration

How to decide whether something is a finding at all, and if it is, how severe it is. Every skill that rates findings uses this file. The short version: **name the boundary and the result, cap severity at the impact you showed, and keep hardening notes out of the findings list.**

This applies to `confirmed` findings only. `needs_validation` items carry blockers and a plan instead of a severity, and `rejected` items carry the control that rules them out (see `findings-format.md` where it ships alongside this file).

## 1. The boundary + result gate

Before a candidate becomes a finding, write down all six of these. Each one has to be concrete, not "an attacker".

| # | Element | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Lower-trust principal**: who starts the attack | Any signed-up user; an unauthenticated internet client; tenant B's admin |
| 2 | **Accepted input**: what they control, and where it enters | The `:id` path segment of `POST /orders/:id/refund` |
| 3 | **Intended control**: what is supposed to stop them | The ownership check that `GET /orders/:id` already performs |
| 4 | **Boundary crossed**: which trust line the input gets across | User A â†’ user B's data |
| 5 | **Affected principal or resource**: who or what gets hurt | Another customer's payment |
| 6 | **Concrete result**: what you observed, or what the traced code does | A refund is issued against an order the caller doesn't own |

If one element is missing:

- **No crossed boundary, or the "victim" is the attacker themselves** (self-XSS, editing your own profile in a weird way, admin doing admin things): it's a hardening note, or nothing.
- **No intended control** that the result defeats: it's a hardening note. A checklist deviation is not a vulnerability by itself.
- **The result depends on a fact outside the code** (proxy rule, IdP setting, deploy flag): it's `needs_validation`, with that fact as the blocker.
- **No concrete result**, only "this could be dangerous": keep tracing, or drop it.

## 2. Likelihood Ã— impact, and overall â‰¤ impact

Rate likelihood and impact separately, each with a one-line reason, then pick an overall.

**Overall may never exceed demonstrated impact.** High likelihood of a low-impact bug is a low finding. If you can't state the concrete damage, the severity is lower than it feels.

### Exploitation signals (dependency and OS-package findings)

For a finding that rests on a published advisory, look up two free signals before rating likelihood, and record them.
Both are public feeds that need no key:

- **CISA KEV** (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities): the CVE is being exploited now. Likelihood is **High**.
- **EPSS** (probability of exploitation in the next 30 days, updated daily): above 0.7, likelihood is **High**;
  0.1 to 0.7, **Medium**; below 0.1, fall back to the CVSS exploitability metrics. These are the same cut points
  `vuln-research` uses.

These signals change **likelihood and the order of work**. They never raise severity above the impact you can show.
KEV plus runtime reachability plus a traced path to the vulnerable function is the strongest case for High or
Critical. A KEV-listed CVE in a build-only or dev-only package stays capped by its impact, but moves to the top of its
severity band: the CI runner or the developer's machine is now what's being attacked.

If a lookup wasn't possible (offline, egress blocked), record the signal as `not checked`. Never infer KEV status from
memory: the catalog grows every week.

### Severity anchors

| Level | Anchor | Typical shape |
|---|---|---|
| **Critical** | Fully defeats a core control with broad, severe consequences and little or no precondition | Pre-auth RCE; auth bypass to any account; cross-tenant read/write of all data; leaked production secret with write authority |
| **High** | **Fully defeats an explicit security control, with real consequences** | IDOR that reads or changes another user's data; privilege escalation to admin; stored XSS that runs in other users' sessions on a sensitive origin; SSRF to cloud metadata credentials |
| **Medium** | **Weakens a control** without fully defeating it, or fully defeats one with limited consequences | Rate limit bypassable only partly; data leak limited to non-sensitive fields; CSRF on a low-value state change; reflected XSS needing unusual interaction |
| **Low** | A real boundary crossing with minor consequences, or one that needs unlikely preconditions | User enumeration with no follow-on; information disclosure of internal hostnames; open redirect that does nothing more on its own |

Low is a finding: something crossed a boundary. **Defense-in-depth is not Low.** It's a hardening note (section 5).

### Availability

The anchors above are written for confidentiality and integrity. For a crash or hang an attacker can cause:

| Level | Shape |
|---|---|
| **High** | One unauthenticated request, or a handful, takes down the whole service or keeps it down: an uncaught exception that kills a single-process server, a ReDoS or `qs`-style parser hang on the main event loop, unbounded memory growth until the process is killed |
| **Medium** | The same, but it needs an account, only hits one worker of several, or the platform restarts it within seconds so the attacker has to keep sending |
| **Low** | It only slows or fails the attacker's own request, or needs volumes that rate limits or the platform already absorb |

Volumetric floods (DDoS) are out of scope for code review. Note the edge protection in the report instead. "Restarts
automatically" lowers likelihood and duration, not the fact that the request crashed it. Keep the restart behaviour
as a `system_configuration` condition, or as a blocker when you can't see it.

The question that separates High from Medium: *does the attack fully defeat the control, and does that cause damage you can name?* If both, High is on the table. If the control is only weakened, or the damage is vague, it's Medium or lower.

## 3. Usually NOT High or Critical

These get over-rated habitually. Rate them High or Critical only when you've traced a specific, severe consequence:

- **Self-XSS**: the only victim is the person typing.
- **Clickjacking** on actions that aren't sensitive.
- **Missing security headers, cookie flags or TLS configuration nits** with no traced exploit path.
- **An open redirect on its own.** It's a phishing aid, not account takeover, until you show the chain.
- **"Could matter if chained"** when the other links are unproven. Rate what you showed, not the hypothetical chain.
- **Anything that already requires admin, shell, or physical access.** Those principals can usually do the damage directly.
- **Session weaknesses that need the attacker to already hold a victim secret** (their cookie, their reset token). Getting that secret is the hard part, and it isn't free.
- **Verbose errors and version banners** without a specific exploitable consequence.
- **Missing rate limiting** where no concrete abuse with real cost has been traced (see below).

### Missing rate limiting

Checklists list rate limiting (OWASP A07, API4), so reviewers find it missing everywhere. Decide it the same way each
time:

- **Finding:** there's no limit in the code on an endpoint where repeated requests do concrete harm. Examples are
  online password guessing against accounts with no lockout, brute-forcing a 6-digit OTP or reset code, and sending
  paid SMS or email, or paid API calls, at the attacker's choice of volume. The intended control is the limit that
  login, OTP and paid-send endpoints are expected to have. Usually Medium, since it weakens authentication rather than
  bypassing it. It's High when the guessable space is small enough to exhaust (a 4- or 6-digit code with no attempt
  limit).
- **`needs_validation`:** the code has no limit, but a gateway, WAF or platform limiter might apply and you can't see
  it. The blocker is that limiter.
- **Hardening note:** endpoints where repetition costs nothing beyond load (search, list, profile reads), or where
  another control already caps the harm (a lockout after N failures).

## 4. High/Critical acceptance checklist

Before you write High or Critical, all six must be true. If any fails, **downgrade rather than delete**: the finding stays, at the level you can defend.

1. **Realistic, in-scope path.** The vulnerable code runs in the deployed product, on a route or job that exists.
2. **Obtainable attacker position.** The principal from the gate can actually get there (open signup counts; "an employee with database access" usually doesn't).
3. **Impact demonstrated, not asserted.** You traced or ran it to the sink and can say what happens there.
4. **Counterevidence found nothing limiting.** The refutation pass looked for the strongest control on the path and didn't find one that stops it.
5. **Concrete reachability evidence.** `file:line` for entrypoint, propagation and sink, or a request/response pair.
6. **Defensible in a debrief.** A skeptical engineer or client would accept the rating after reading the evidence. Anchor test: *would serious triage accept this as High?*

### Missing deployment evidence

When the decisive fact lives in the deployment (is there a WAF? does the proxy strip this header?), that lowers **confidence**, not the severity floor. Either record it as `needs_validation` with the fact as a blocker, or keep the severity you traced and set confidence to `medium` or `low`. Don't quietly mark a traced High as Low because you couldn't see production.

## 5. Hardening notes are not findings

A **hardening note** is a gap with no traced impact: defense in depth, a best-practice deviation, a missing header with no exploit path, a cookie flag that changes nothing reachable.

- If layer A prevents the attack, the absence of layer B is a hardening note.
- Hardening notes **never get a severity** and don't go in `findings.json`.
- They go in a separate report section titled **"Hardening notes (not findings)"**, one line each: what's missing, why it would help, and the effort.
- Headers, cookie flags and CORS settings become findings only when you trace a concrete impact (e.g. a permissive CORS policy that, combined with credentialed requests, lets an attacker origin read a user's data).

Reporting hardening notes separately keeps the findings list credible. A report where half the "Lows" are missing headers trains readers to skip the Lows.

## 6. Keys: publishable vs restricted vs secret

A public identifier called a "key" is not a secret. Before rating an exposed key, find out which kind it is and what it can do:

| Kind | Examples | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| **Publishable** (designed to ship to browsers or apps) | Stripe `pk_live_â€¦`, Firebase web config, Google Maps browser keys, Supabase `anon` key, Sentry DSN | Not a finding by itself. A finding only if its restrictions are missing and that enables real abuse (e.g. an unrestricted Maps key billed to you, or a Supabase `anon` key in front of tables with no row-level security), and then rate that consequence |
| **Restricted** (scoped server key) | Stripe `rk_â€¦`, a read-only API token | Rate by the scope it grants |
| **Secret** (full authority) | Stripe `sk_live_â€¦`, AWS secret access key, Supabase `service_role`, database URL with password | Rate by the authority: production write access is usually High or Critical |

The prefix alone doesn't decide it. `AIzaâ€¦` is the format of many Google API keys; some are meant to be public and some unlock paid APIs. Check what the key is restricted to before rating.

## 7. Severity vs SLA

Severity describes the bug. The remediation deadline (SLA) is a policy decision your org attaches to a severity. Keep them in separate columns. A deferral changes the deadline, never the severity.

# Verification â€” Per-Finding Refutation Pass

Shared reference for audit skills (`owasp-audit`, `api-audit`, `business-logic-testing`, `web-pentest`) and for
`finding-triage`. Every candidate finding goes through this pass **before** it reaches `findings.json` or a report.
The goal is to try to disprove the candidate, then close it with one of three verdicts.

The pass works because the person checking a finding is not the person who found it. Someone who wrote the candidate
tends to re-read their own reasoning instead of the code. A verifier that only sees the claim and the cited lines
reads the code.

## Two stages: fixed exclusions, then the verifier

False positives get filtered twice, in this order.

**Stage 1: fixed exclusion rules.** Before any verifier runs, drop the candidates that match a rule below. The rules
are mechanical and the same on every run, so two runs over the same code drop the same candidates. Apply them by where
the code lives and whether it ships, never by how likely the bug looks.

| Rule | Drops a candidate in | Unless |
|---|---|---|
| Test code | `test/`, `tests/`, `spec/`, `__tests__/`, `*.test.*`, `*.spec.*`, `*_test.go`, `test_*.py` | Production code imports it, the route or handler is mounted in the deployed build, or the build ships the file |
| Fixtures and sample data | `fixtures/`, `testdata/`, `__mocks__/`, seed files for local dev | The deployed environment loads it (a production seed, a default config read at boot) |
| Generated code | Files marked `Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT` or `@generated`, compiled output (`dist/`, `build/`, `.next/`) | Never. Raise it against the generator input or template instead, which is where the fix goes |
| Vendored and third-party code | `vendor/`, `node_modules/`, `third_party/`, copied-in libraries | The repo has modified the copy. An unmodified copy is a version question for `dependency-audit` |
| Docs and examples | `*.md`, `docs/`, `examples/`, snippets in comments | The example is deployed, or the repo's own code copies it |
| Documented hardening note | The gap is already on the run's hardening-notes list | The candidate brings a traced impact the note didn't have. Then it's a new candidate |
| Prior rejection | The fingerprint matches a `rejected` record from the last run | The code at `ruled_out_by.location` changed. Then it's a new candidate |

Some things are never excluded by location. A credential that looks live is a finding wherever it sits, including a
test fixture (`secrets-audit` owns it). CI workflow files run with real tokens, so they are not "config". A debug or
test route is in scope as soon as the deployed build serves it.

Record what stage 1 dropped and which rule dropped it: a count per rule in the report, and, where the skill keeps a
coverage ledger, an `out_of_scope` unit whose check names the rule. Excluded candidates get no `findings.json` record.

**Stage 2: the per-finding verifier.** Every candidate that survives stage 1 goes through the pass below. The verifier
does not invent new exclusions. "It's probably test code" is a stage 1 question with a fixed answer, not a reason a
verifier can give.

This repo deliberately does not drop whole bug classes in stage 1. Some filters exclude every denial-of-service,
rate-limiting or open-redirect report outright. Several skills here report those and calibrate severity instead (see
`severity-calibration.md`), so class-level filtering would hide real findings.

## When to run it

- After the checklist / hunting phase, once per candidate. Don't batch several candidates into one verifier: a
  verifier that rejects one candidate tends to wave the next one through.
- **Small targets** (a few thousand lines, a dozen or more candidates): one verifier per candidate can mean 20
  subagents for a 150-line app. There you may group candidates that share no code path, up to about five per
  verifier, with each candidate written up and closed separately. Two candidates stay in separate verifiers when they
  touch the same handler or control, or when either one would be confirmed at High or Critical.
- Again whenever a verdict would move **up** (rejected â†’ needs_validation, needs_validation â†’ confirmed, or a
  severity increase) or the evidence changes materially. **An upgrade needs a new, independent verifier.** The verifier
  that produced the lower verdict does not get to overturn itself.
- On re-runs, for every carried-forward confirmed finding whose code changed (see `orchestration.md` where present).

A downgrade (confirmed â†’ needs_validation, or a lower severity) can be applied directly. Record why.

## How to run it

**With subagents** (Claude Code `Task`/Agent tool, or any platform that can spawn an isolated agent): spawn one fresh
verifier per candidate. Give it **only**:

1. The candidate record: title, claimed location, `trace[]`, `evidence[]`, and the claimed impact
2. Read access to the repository
3. The verdict definitions and the "does NOT rule out" list below
4. The record shape it must return (see `findings-format.md` where present)

Do **not** pass the hunter's reasoning, chat history, or the rest of the report.

In Claude Code with this plugin installed, use the plugin's `finding-verifier` subagent. It carries this procedure, the
rationalizations table below and the return shape, and it has only `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob`. Give it one candidate per
call. Other platforms use the template below.

**Without subagents** (single-context agents, Cursor, Codex): run the pass as a separate, explicit step after hunting
is finished. For each candidate, start from the cited `file:line` and re-derive the path from scratch. Don't re-read
your own earlier notes about the candidate until you have written down a verdict.

### Verifier prompt (template)

Adapt this to the platform. Keep the substance.

```text
You are verifying a security finding that someone else wrote. Assume it is wrong until the code proves otherwise.
Your job is to refute it.

Candidate:
<candidate record: title, location, trace[], evidence[], claimed impact>

Do this:
1. Open every file:line cited in trace[] and evidence[]. Confirm each line says what the candidate claims.
   If a cited line does not exist or says something else, note it.
2. Walk the path from the entrypoint to the sink. At each hop, list every control that could stop the attack:
   middleware, auth/ownership checks, validation, type coercion, framework escaping, database constraints,
   platform config in the repo.
3. Name the STRONGEST control you found. For that control, decide: does it run on EVERY path an attacker can reach
   before the sink, at the right time, and fail closed?
4. Decide whether the claimed impact actually follows. Who is the lower-trust principal, what boundary is crossed,
   and what concrete result occurs?
5. Return exactly one verdict: confirmed | needs_validation | rejected, with the fields listed for that verdict.
   Fill `counterevidence` with what you tried and what you found, even when the verdict is confirmed.
```

## The three verdicts

| Verdict | Bar | Required fields | Severity? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `confirmed` | A complete trace from attacker-controlled entrypoint â†’ (missing or bypassable control) â†’ sink â†’ concrete impact, **or** a working proof-of-concept against an environment you're authorized to test | `trace[]` (entrypoint first, sink last), `evidence[]`, `counterevidence`, `confidence`, `severity`, `conditions[]` | Yes |
| `needs_validation` | The code supports the claim, but **one decisive fact lives outside the code**: proxy or CDN behaviour, IdP settings, deploy-time env, a managed-service default, the headers a deployed origin actually sends | `blockers[]` (each names the exact unknown fact), `validation_plan` (a check the owner can run), `counterevidence`, `confidence` | **No.** Severity is assigned only after the blocker resolves to confirmed |
| `rejected` | A **specific named control, at a specific location**, runs on **every** path an attacker can reach before the sink and fails closed | `ruled_out_by {control, location}`, `counterevidence` | No |

### confirmed

- The trace has to be complete. "User input reaches `exec()`" is not a trace until you show where the input enters,
  each hop, and why nothing on the way stops it.
- `confidence` is honest. **A static-only trace caps at `medium`.** `high` needs a reproduced PoC, a failing test, or
  equivalent runtime evidence, recorded as `"reproduced": true` (the validator rejects `high` without it). Missing deployment evidence lowers confidence; it does not lower the severity floor of
  what the code demonstrably does.
- Severity follows [severity-calibration.md](severity-calibration.md): likelihood Ã— impact, and `overall â‰¤ impact`. If you can't state the
  concrete damage, the severity is lower than it feels.
- Record `conditions[]` that limit exploitation (`authentication_level`, `authorization_role`, `user_interaction`,
  `system_configuration`, `network_routing`, `environmental_dependency`, `data_state`, `timing_dependency`,
  `third_party_dependency`).

### needs_validation

This replaces the old "Potential" label. It is **not** a parking place for a hunch. Use it only when the code really does
support the claim and a single external fact decides it.

- Each `blockers[]` entry names one fact: "Whether Vercel strips `x-forwarded-host` before it reaches the app",
  not "deployment config unknown".
- `validation_plan` is a check the **owner** can run, local and/or against their deployment, with the expected result
  for each outcome. Example:

  ```text
  Run against your production origin:  curl -sI https://app.example.com/embed | grep -iE 'x-frame-options|content-security-policy'
  If both `frame-ancestors *` and `X-Frame-Options: DENY` appear â†’ confirmed (contradictory framing policy).
  If only one appears â†’ rejected; ruled out by the deployed header set.
  ```

- If you can't write a blocker and a plan, the candidate is either confirmed (you already know enough) or it's a
  hardening note or a rejected claim. It isn't needs_validation.

### rejected

- Name the control and where it lives: `ruled_out_by: { control: "requireOrgMember() guard", location:
  "src/server/trpc.ts:41" }`. "Looks safe" or "framework handles it" is not a rejection.
- The control must sit on **every** reachable path, run **before** the sink, and **fail closed**.
- Keep rejected records in `findings.json`. Re-runs read them so the same claim isn't raised again. A rejection
  suppresses **only that exact claim** (same fingerprint). A sibling path or a changed control is a new candidate.

Some rejections have no guard to point at. `ruled_out_by` then names the fact that rules the claim out and
`location` points at the evidence for it:

| Why it's ruled out | `control` | `location` |
|---|---|---|
| Never reached: the vulnerable function or package is never called | "`_.template` is never called; lodash is used only for `merge` and `pick`" | The only import or call site of the package. If nothing imports it, the line in the manifest or lockfile that declares it |
| Known-inert value: a vendor's published example key, a documented test card, a placeholder | "AWS's documented example access key ID; it can't authenticate" | The line where the value appears |
| Control inside a dependency: the library's own guard runs on every path | "jsonwebtoken 9.0.2 `verify()` rejects `alg: none` when a secret is given" | The lockfile or manifest line that pins that version |

A control inside a dependency rejects only when the installed version is pinned and that version's behaviour is the
one you checked: read in the vendored or installed source, the changelog, or the advisory's fixed-in version. If the
range in the manifest could resolve to a version without the guard and there's no lockfile, it's `needs_validation`
with the resolved version as the blocker. "The library probably handles it" is not a rejection (see below).

## What does NOT rule out a candidate

None of these is a reason to reject. Each one is a reason to keep looking:

- **General trust in a library or framework** ("Prisma parameterizes", "React escapes") without checking that this call
  site uses the safe API. Raw-query escape hatches and `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` exist for a reason.
- **A control on a different path.** The REST route checks ownership. The server action that writes the same table
  doesn't.
- **A control that runs at the wrong time.** Validation after the side effect, auth checked at enqueue but not in the
  worker, a signature verified after the body was already stored.
- **A control that can fail open.** Unset env var interpolation, `catch {}` around the check, a rate limiter that
  allows on Redis error, a feature flag defaulting to off.
- **A safe sibling.** Three handlers use the guard. That says nothing about the fourth.
- **Missing information.** "I couldn't find where this is called" is a blocker or an unresolved coverage item. It isn't
  a rejection.
- **Difficulty.** "Requires guessing a UUID" or "requires a race" lowers likelihood. It doesn't remove the finding.
- **The setting is operator-configurable.** If the shipped default is unsafe, the default is the finding (see "Unsafe
  shipped defaults" below).
- **"It's internal."** Internal services get reached through SSRF, compromised neighbours, and misrouted ingress.
  Record the network assumption as a `network_routing` condition instead.
- **Tests pass.** Tests check intended behaviour, not adversarial input.

## Rationalizations to reject

The list above says what can't close a candidate. This table is for the verifier's own reasoning, in both directions.
Each row is an argument that feels like a conclusion but isn't one, and the evidence that would actually settle it.
When you notice yourself making one of these arguments, go and get that evidence. If you can't get it, the
argument doesn't change the verdict.

Models in particular lean toward seeing bugs and toward rating them high. The verifier's default is that the candidate
is wrong. A verifier can also overcorrect, and wave things through to get to a clean report. Both columns matter.

**Arguments for keeping or inflating a candidate**

| Rationalization | What settles it |
|---|---|
| "This pattern is dangerous, so it's a vulnerability" | A trace from an attacker-reachable entrypoint to this call site, with the attacker's value still able to do harm when it gets there. A dangerous sink with no reachable input is not a finding |
| "An attacker could theoreticallyâ€¦" | Name the lower-trust principal, the exact input they send, and the line where it enters. Every "if" in the story is either shown in the code, recorded as a `conditions[]` entry, or written as a `needs_validation` blocker |
| "This is clearly critical" | The concrete damage, stated in one sentence, and the High/Critical acceptance checks in `severity-calibration.md`. `overall` stays at or below the impact you can show |
| "The same bug is in the sibling handler" | This call site, read on its own. A sibling's bug doesn't transfer, any more than a sibling's guard does |
| "It could matter if chained" | Each link in the chain shown in the code. Any unproven link makes it a blocker or a hardening note |
| "There's no input validation here" | What the sink does with the values that can actually reach it. A missing check on a value that's already typed, bounded or mapped through an allow-list may have no impact |
| "The scanner, the report or the code comment says it's vulnerable" | The code that runs. Claim text, `TODO: fix auth` comments and rule names are leads, not evidence |

**Arguments for dismissing a candidate**

| Rationalization | What settles it |
|---|---|
| "The framework probably escapes this" | This call site uses the safe API: auto-escaping is on in the config you can see and this output isn't marked raw, or the query goes through the parameterized builder rather than a raw-query method. Name the file and line |
| "There's probably a WAF, gateway or proxy in front" | The rule in the repo or IaC, applied to this route. If it lives outside the repo, it's `needs_validation` with the rule as the blocker. Never `rejected` on "probably" |
| "It's only internal" | Network policy, ingress or security-group config in the repo showing no path from the lower-trust principal. Without it, record a `network_routing` condition and keep the verdict |
| "The test suite would have caught it" | A test that sends this adversarial input to this path, asserts it's refused, and runs in CI. Cite its file and line. Even then, it settles only the path it exercises |
| "It's validated upstream" | The validator's file and line, shown to run on every path to this sink, before the sink, and to fail closed. That's the `rejected` bar. Short of it, keep looking |
| "The UI never sends that value" | A server-side check. Clients are attacker-controlled, so what the form allows proves nothing |
| "It's behind auth" | Authentication isn't authorization. Show the ownership or role check, or the finding stands with an `authentication_level` condition |
| "Only admins can reach it" | The role check's location, then ask whether the admin crosses any boundary (another tenant, a higher role, the host). Admin to admin on the admin's own data is no boundary. Admin to another tenant is |
| "The IDs are UUIDs, nobody can guess them" | Whether the IDs leak through list endpoints, URLs, logs, emails or referrers. Difficulty lowers likelihood. It doesn't reject |
| "This code looks unused" | The never-reached row of the table under "rejected": no call site, route not mounted. Point at the evidence. "Looks unused" alone is a blocker, not a rejection |
| "I already rejected something like this" | Nothing. Each candidate is checked on its own facts. This is why candidates get one verifier each |

## Unsafe shipped defaults

A hard-coded fallback secret (`process.env.JWT_SECRET || "changeme"`), a debug flag that defaults on, or a permissive
default config is **`confirmed`**, not `needs_validation`, whichever skill finds it. The code shows what happens
whenever the setting is missing, and missing is the state a new deployment starts in.

- Record a `system_configuration` condition: "deployments that don't set `JWT_SECRET`, or set it empty".
- Rate severity by what the default gives an attacker, as if it were live. Whether production overrides it is a
  deployment fact you can't see, so it caps `confidence` at `medium`. It doesn't lower the verdict or the severity.
- Put the owner's check (is the variable set, and to what length) in the finding's fix-verification text, not in a
  `validation_plan`.
- If you *can* see the deployment and it sets a strong value, the record is still `confirmed`, since a fresh deploy
  or a new environment gets the default. Rate likelihood lower and say why.

The same root cause should get the same verdict and severity from every skill that sees it. A hard-coded JWT fallback
that lets anyone forge an admin token is an authentication bypass to any account, wherever it's reported.

## Hardening notes are not verdicts

If the verifier finds the gap is real but there's **no traced impact** (Layer A already stops the attack and Layer B is
missing; a missing header with no exploit path; a checklist deviation), close the candidate as a **Hardening note**. It
goes in the report's "Hardening notes (not findings)" section with no severity. It gets no `findings.json` record.
Keep hardening notes in a short list next to the JSON (for example `hardening-notes.md` in the audit output directory)
so the report can render them. The coverage unit that produced the note can still be `covered`.

If a hardening note later picks up a traced impact (say, a missing CSP turns out to matter because a stored XSS sink
exists), it becomes a new candidate and goes through this pass.

## Live probing

Live checks stay allowed **when authorized**. For example, `curl -I` against the user's own deployed origin, or
confirming that a leaked key is live as part of secrets triage. The rules:

1. The authorization check of the consuming skill applies to the live target, not just the source. Only probe hosts
   the user owns or is authorized to test, and only with non-destructive requests (`HEAD`/`GET`, no state changes, no
   real customer credentials).
2. **A check you describe but don't run is a `needs_validation` item.** Write the exact command into
   `validation_plan`. Don't mark it confirmed or rejected on the strength of what the config file "should" produce.
3. A check you actually ran becomes evidence. Record the command, timestamp, and relevant response lines in
   `evidence[]` / `counterevidence`, then close the verdict normally.
4. For paired evidence (baseline request next to attack request), see `web-pentest`.

## Output of the pass

For each candidate, one record with the verdict-specific fields above, ready to be written to `findings.json`. The
consuming skill writes `findings.json`, validates it (`validate-findings.mjs` where present), and renders the report
from it. Prose never changes a verdict, severity, blocker, or demonstrated impact. If the report and the JSON disagree,
the JSON wins and the report is regenerated.

### Rules the validator enforces

- Top level is an array, sorted by `fingerprint` in plain code-unit order (`jq 'sort_by(.fingerprint)'` gives the same order for ASCII ids). No duplicate fingerprints.
- Shape per verdict, with no extra fields. `severity` and `disposition` appear only on `confirmed`.
- Paths are repo-relative with forward slashes: no leading `/`, drive letter, `~`, URL, backslash or `..` segment.
- Every `line` is an integer â‰¥ 1.
- Trace order (entrypoint first, sink last). `overall` â‰¤ impact. `high` confidence on `confirmed` needs `reproduced: true`.
- `needs_validation` has non-empty `blockers` and `validation_plan`. `rejected` has `ruled_out_by`.

### Skill-specific fields (`ext`)

Some skills need fields the common shape doesn't have: the PCI DSS requirement a gap is against, the cloud account and region of a resource, the MASVS control, the HIPAA standard. Those go in `ext`, never as new top-level fields (the validator rejects unknown fields). Each skill lists its `ext` keys in its own SKILL.md.

- Keys are snake_case (`requirement`, `in_cde`, `account`). Values are a non-empty string, a number, a boolean, or a non-empty array of those. No nesting, no `null`, no empty `ext` (leave it out instead).
- Don't repeat what already has a field. The CWE goes in `cwe`, the OWASP category in `owasp_category`, the file in `location`.
- `to-sarif.mjs` copies `ext` into the SARIF result's `properties.ext` unchanged.

```json
"ext": { "requirement": "8.4.2", "in_cde": true }
```

`finding-triage` adds three keys to any confirmed record it closes as `Fixed`, next to the producing skill's own: `fixed_in` (the fixing commit SHA or release tag), `fix_verified_on` (`YYYY-MM-DD`, when the fix check passed against the shipped fix) and `regression_test` (repo-relative path or array of paths). A record that regresses loses `disposition`, `fixed_in` and `fix_verified_on`, and gets `regressed_after` with the old `fixed_in` value. Skills shouldn't use these four names for anything else.

### Findings about deployed resources

Not every finding lives in a source file. A cloud bucket policy, an IdP setting, a live host's TLS configuration or a decompiled app binary still needs a `location`. Save the read-only output that shows the problem into the audit's output directory, then point `location` and `evidence[]` at that file and line:

```text
security-audit/evidence/aws-s3-get-bucket-policy-prod-assets.json   # aws s3api get-bucket-policy ... > this file
```

- Redact before saving. Never write a secret value, a session token or customer data into an evidence file.
- Record the command and the time it ran in the evidence `description`, so the owner can run it again.
- Build the fingerprint from the resource's own id, with slashes: `cloud-audit/s3-public-read/aws/123456789012/prod-assets`. ARNs and `host:port` contain `:<digits>`, which the validator reads as a line number.

## Fingerprints

A fingerprint names the root cause, so the same bug keeps the same id after code moves, severity changes, or the verdict flips. A good pattern:

```
<skill>/<cwe-or-class>/<repo-relative file>/<function, route, or resource>
api-audit/CWE-639/src/routes/orders.ts/refundOrder
secrets-audit/aws-access-key/config/deploy.yml/AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
dependency-audit/GHSA-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx/package-lock.json/lodash
```

If a file is renamed, keep the old fingerprint when it's obviously the same root cause. Don't put the line number, the date or the severity in it.

# Orchestration â€” Modes, Run Profiles, Hunters, and Re-runs

Shared reference for `owasp-audit` and `api-audit`. Use it when an audit is too big for one pass, or when the user asks
for a full audit. It assumes the recon and ledger from [recon-and-coverage.md](recon-and-coverage.md), the verdicts from [verification.md](verification.md),
and the record format in [findings-format.md](findings-format.md).

A single audit pass finds a fraction of what repeated, independent passes find. Cloudflare reports that one run
surfaced roughly half of what several runs found together. Splitting the work and repeating it is how you close that
gap. The evidence bar stays the same.

## Operating modes

| Mode | When | Output |
|---|---|---|
| **Guidance** (default) | The user asks a question, wants a quick look at a file or feature, or wants to know how to secure something | Conversational answer. Findings still follow the verdict rules. No ledger required |
| **Full audit** | The user explicitly asks for an audit / security review of a codebase, a PR, or a release | Recon â†’ ledger â†’ hunting â†’ verification â†’ critic â†’ `findings.json` â†’ report |

If the request is ambiguous ("can you check this for security issues?" on a whole repo), ask one question first: *"Do
you want a quick guidance pass, or a full audit with a coverage ledger and a findings.json report?"* Then proceed.

## Run profiles

Ask which profile, or pick one and say so. The report header names the profile.

| Profile | Hunting | Critic | Verification | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `quick` | One wave over the highest-priority units | One critic wave; leftovers become `deferred` | One independent verifier per candidate | Pre-launch smoke check, small app, time-boxed |
| `standard` | Waves until every in-scope unit is `covered`, `candidate`, `not_applicable`, or justified `deferred` | Repeat until a wave adds nothing high-value | One verifier per candidate, and a new one for any upgrade | Default full audit |
| `deep` | As standard, plus a Wildcard and an Obvious-things hunter, plus a second independent hunter on high-value boundaries | Repeat until a critic wave returns **no** missing units | As standard; also re-verify every confirmed high/critical with a second verifier | Pre-raise diligence, regulated data, after an incident |
